newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian shares take breather, to rise again-trade.
newsitem.headline: Russian shares take breather, to rise again-trade.

text.p: Leading Russian shares paused for a breather on Thursday after heady gains this week, but some traders said the market would renew its climb in coming days.
The Russian Trading System (RTS) index gained 1.67 percent to 184.67 on $28.2 million in traded volume.
Mosenergo closed at $0.99, down from $1.02 at Wednesday's close. Gazprom closed higher at $0.480 after $0.461 and LUKoil finished up at $10.60 after $10.25.

Robert Devane of Troika-Dialog said the market would gain ground in coming weeks but that it could later lose ground closer to the date of President Boris Yeltsin's bypass heart operation, expected in the next couple of months.
"It is highly unlikely the market will continue its run-up through the surgery," he said, predicting a bell curve of growth and then fall, potentially below Thursday's levels.
"The trigger for the emotional volatility will be the Yeltsin surgery."
He said recent market gains put prices on par with those seen just before Yeltsin announced on September 5 that he would undergo surgery.
"Most of the gain over the last few trading sessions is really a recovery from that dip," he said. The RTS index closed at 185.00 on September 4, the day before Yeltsin's announcement.

Traders were not surprised by the market as Russian investors and brokers took profits after the RTS's record volume on Wedneday for the calendar year of $47 million and the RTS Index's gain of nearly seven percent.
Martin Diggle of Brunswick declined to call the market's short-term direction, but said that it would largely gather steam through 1997.
"MinFin bonds are up 60 to 70 percent over election levels, but the equities market is still 10 percent below," he said.
"There may be some strategic moves from bonds to equities, and domestic funds will be switching from Treasury bills (GKOs) as well."

He said a recent spate of good market news -- including lower GKO yields, a good rating for Russia ahead of its Eurobond offer and the launch of an International Finance Corporation Russia index -- would bring new money into the market.

But traders said an expected "wall of money" would not materialise before Christmas and that Western institutional investors would re-allocate funds and heavily invest in Russia no earlier than January or February 1997.
Devane said some secondary stocks, including river transport companies, were piquing investors' interest.
